newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso effectively devalued, shares leap.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso effectively devalued, shares leap.

text.p: The Philippines on Friday unnerved currency markets in Asia after it caved in to unbearable pressure and effectively devalued the peso.
It became the second Asian country in two weeks to succumb to currency speculators, following in the footsteps of Thailand which was forced into a de facto devaluation of the baht last week.

The Philippine central bank's surprise decision to allow the peso to move in a wider range to the dollar saw the local currency lose 11.5 percent, boosting share prices by the biggest one-day rise in some seven years.

The peso slumped to 29.45 per dollar following the announcement this morning, before the Bankers Association of the Philippines suspended trading for the day. The level was the weakest for the local unit in nearly four years.

The central bank's move to loosen controls on the peso came after heavy speculative selling of the currency in the past two weeks and repeated denials by Philippine authorities that they were considering a devaluation.
Central bank intervention to fend off speculators rapidly ate up currency reserves and forced up interest rates to levels analysts said would hurt the economy.
However, Philippine shares responded to the peso's losses by soaring nearly seven percent after a four-day slide.

"The whole pattern has been reversed and the public is back into equities. Unexpectedly, the market went boom. This just goes to show you that the market is not dead," said Irving Ackerman, president at I. Ackerman & Co Inc.
President Fidel Ramos issued a statement backing the central bank's action, insisting it was not a devaluation.
He made no reference to his comments earlier in the week that "outsiders" were deliberately trying to undermine the peso.

"This exchange rate action reaffirms the goverment's commitment to do whatever is necessary to sustain our economic growth, control inflation and generate employment through, among others, the protection of our international reserves," he said.

The move immediately won the praise of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Michel Camdessus who called it timely and decisive and he would recommend the IMF board agree to extend its Extended Fund Facility to the Philippines.
The central bank, which hopes it has now put an end to speculation against its currency, said the lower peso should not damage the economy and that it expected interest rates to ease.
It said the economy would not suffer, but admitted it could not afford to defend the peso much longer.
Some bankers estimate the bank has spent up to $2 billion, or about 17 percent of the reserves it had, to defend its currency from the spillover effect of Thailand's financial crisis.
The Philippine move shook the currency markets of its neighbours, helping send the Thai baht to a new low and rattling currency traders in Indonesia and Malaysia.
The Philippine Bankers' Association invoked a rule not used in two years by which it does not recognise the effective devaluation.

Under its rules which govern peso trading among local banks, the rate cannot move more than 1-1/2 percent in either direction of a weighted average, calculated from the closing rate of the previous day.
Any trades outside that will not be officially recognised.

Its average rate for the resumption of trading on Monday will be 26.40 pesos per dollar, and since it was highly certain the peso will move well below that, trading will have to be suspended again almost as soon as it restarts, traders said.
Reaction to the central bank move was mixed with businessmen welcoming the end to punitive interest rates while some bankers said the central bank had lost all credibility.

"They (the authorities) were very consistent in that they agreed to allow the peso to weaken on a gradual but orderly basis," said Jaime Panganiban, Bank of America head of treasury in Manila. "Today they destroyed that credibility. This will really be a big setback for this market in the eyes of the world."
One drawback could be for Philippine companies which have up to $5 billion in oustanding foreign currency loans. They will now have to find more pesos to pay off those loans.
But the president of the Philippines Federation of Industries, Raul Concepcion, welcomed the move, saying that high interest rates to defend the peso were hurting business.
Overnight interest rates have doubled to 32 percent in the past two weeks and prime lending rates hit 21 percent.

"We're pleased that the central bank has decided to allow free market forces to come in...they couldn't continue to defend (the peso) with high interest rates because loans from commercial banks had jumped from 13 to 21 percent."
"If this were to continue the penalty to industry of higher interest rates would certainly be far greater than keeping the exchange rate at 26.40," he told Reuters Financial Television.
